fields.title: Humility
fields.description: Andrew Murray explores the profound wisdom of humility, countering self-promotion in a world obsessed with it. He reveals humility’s three motives: as creatures, sinners, and saints, drawing inspiration from heavenly hosts, Jesus, and God’s grace. Murray challenges misconceptions, emphasizing humility as participation in Christ’s life and the highest fulfillment of our destiny. Contents: The Glory of The Creature—The Secret of Redemption—Humility in the Life of Jesus—Humility in the Teaching of Jesus—Humility in the Disciples of Jesus—Humility in the Daily Life—Humility and Holiness—Humility and Sin—Humility and Faith—Humility and Death to Self —Humility and Happiness—Humility and Exaltation—A Prayer for Humility.

fields.title: The Glory of the Creature
fields.body_html:
“Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honour and power, for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created.” Rev. 4:11.

When God created the universe, He had one purpose: to let His creatures share in His perfection and joy, and so to show in them the glory of His love, wisdom and power. God wanted to reveal Himself in and through the beings He made by giving them as much of His own goodness and glory as they could receive. But He did not hand the creature something it could own by itself — a portion of life or goodness for it to keep and manage on its own. Not at all. God is the ever-living, ever-present, ever-acting One, who holds all things together by His powerful word and in whom all things exist. So the creature’s relationship to God could only be one of constant, complete and universal dependence. Just as surely as God once created by His power, so by that same power He must sustain every creature at every moment.

The creature must not only look back to where its existence began and admit that it owes everything to God. Its chief care, its highest virtue and its only happiness, now and for all eternity, is to offer itself as an empty vessel in which God can live and show His power and goodness.

The life God gives is not given once for all. It is given moment by moment, through the unceasing work of His mighty power. Humility — the place of complete dependence on God — is therefore, by the very nature of things, the creature’s first duty and highest virtue, and the root of every other virtue.

So pride, the loss of this humility, is the root of every sin and every evil. The angels who fell began by looking at themselves with satisfaction; that led them to disobey, and they were thrown down from the light of heaven into outer darkness. In the same way, when the serpent breathed the poison of his pride — the desire to be like God — into the hearts of our first parents, they too fell from their high position into all the misery in which humanity now lies. In heaven and on earth, pride and self-exaltation are the gateway to hell, its origin and its curse.

Nothing can redeem us except the restoring of that lost humility — the original and only true relationship of the creature to its God. That is why Jesus came: to bring humility back to earth, to let us share in it, and by it to save us. In heaven He humbled Himself to become a man. The humility we see in Him was already His in heaven; it brought Him here, and He brought it with Him. Here on earth “He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8). His humility gave His death its worth, and so became our redemption. And the salvation He now gives is nothing less and nothing other than a sharing of His own life and death, His own attitude and spirit, His own humility — the very ground and root of His relationship to God and of His work of redemption.

Jesus Christ took humanity’s place and fulfilled what a creature was meant to be by living a life of perfect humility. His humility is our salvation, and His salvation is our humility. The lives of those who are saved, the lives of the saints, must carry this mark of rescue from sin and full restoration to what they were made to be: their whole relationship to God and to people shaped by a humility that runs through everything. Without it there can be no real living in God’s presence and no experience of His favour or of the power of His Spirit. Instead, faith, love, joy and strength will fail to last.

Humility is the only soil in which the graces can take root. A lack of humility is enough to explain every weakness and every failure. Humility is not simply one grace or virtue alongside the others; it is the root of them all, because it alone is the right attitude before God — the attitude that lets Him do everything as God. God has made us reasoning beings, so the more clearly we see the real nature of a command and how absolutely it is needed, the more readily and fully we will obey it. The call to humility has been given too little attention in the Church because its true nature and importance have been too little understood.

Humility is not something we bring to God, nor something He hands to us. It is simply the sense of being nothing that comes when we see how truly God is everything — and in that sense we make room for God to be everything. When the creature realises that this is its true dignity, and consents to it with its will, its mind and its affections, it becomes the vessel in which God’s life and glory can work and show themselves. Humility, it then sees, is simply admitting the truth about its position as a creature and yielding to God.

In the lives of earnest Christians — those who pursue and profess holiness — humility ought to be the chief sign of their sincerity. People often say that it is not. Could one reason be that, in the Church’s teaching and example, humility has never been given the supreme place that belongs to it? And could that, in turn, come from neglecting this truth: that strong as sin is as a reason for humility, there is a reason with an even wider and mightier influence — the one that makes the angels humble, that made Jesus humble, and that makes the holiest saints in heaven so humble?

The first and chief mark of the creature’s relationship to God, and the secret of its happiness, is a humility and nothingness that leaves God free to be all in all. I am sure many Christians will admit that their experience has been much like mine: we knew the Lord for a long time without realising that gentleness and lowliness of heart are meant to be the distinguishing mark of the disciple, as they were of the Master. Nor did we realise that this humility does not come by itself, but must be made the object of special desire, prayer, faith and practice.

As we study the Bible, we will see how clearly and how often Jesus taught His disciples about this, and how slow they were to understand Him. So, at the very start of these meditations, let us admit that nothing is as natural to us, nothing as subtle and hidden from our sight, and nothing as difficult and dangerous as pride.

Let us accept that only determination and perseverance, as we wait on God and on Christ, will show us how much we lack the grace of humility, and how powerless we are to obtain what we seek.

Let us study the character of Christ until our souls are filled with love and admiration for His lowliness. And let us believe that when we are broken by the sense of our pride and our helplessness to drive it out, Jesus Christ Himself will come in and give us this grace too, as part of His wonderful life within us.

Note A. All this is to make known to every region of eternity that pride can turn the highest angels into devils, and humility can raise fallen flesh and blood to the thrones of angels. This is the great purpose of God raising a new creation out of a fallen kingdom of angels. That is why it stands in a state of war between the fire and pride of the fallen angels and the humility of the Lamb of God: so that the last trumpet may sound this great truth through the depths of eternity — evil can have no beginning except from pride, and no end except from humility.

The truth is this: either pride dies in you, or nothing of heaven can live in you. Under the banner of this truth, give yourself up to the gentle and humble spirit of the holy Jesus. Humility must sow the seed, or there can be no harvest in heaven. Do not look at pride as merely an unattractive temper, or at humility as merely a respectable virtue. One is death and the other is life; one is all hell and the other is all heaven. As much pride as you have in you, that much of the fallen angels is alive in you; as much true humility as you have, that much of the Lamb of God you have within you.

If you could see what every stirring of pride does to your soul, you would beg everything you meet to tear that snake away from you, even at the cost of a hand or an eye. If you could see what a sweet, divine, transforming power there is in humility — how it drives out the poison of your nature and makes room for the Spirit of God to live in you — you would rather be the footstool of the whole world than lack even the smallest degree of it. —William Law, The Spirit of Prayer, Part II, p. 73 (Moreton edition, Canterbury, 1893).

fields.title: The Secret of Redemption
fields.body_html:
“Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus, who, though he was in the form of God, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God has highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name.” Philippians 2:5-9.

No tree can grow except from the root it sprang from. All its life long, it can only live with the life that was in the seed that produced it. Grasping this truth fully, and applying it to the first Adam and the Second, helps us understand both why we need the redemption that is in Jesus and what that redemption is. The old serpent had been thrown out of heaven for his pride; his whole nature as the devil was pride. When he spoke his tempting words into Eve’s ear, those words carried the very poison of hell.

When she listened, and let her desire and her will reach for the prospect of being like God, knowing good and evil, the poison entered her soul, her blood and her life. It destroyed for ever that blessed humility and dependence on God that would have been our everlasting happiness. Because of this, her life, and the life of the whole human race descended from her, became corrupted to its very root with Satan’s own pride — the most terrible of all sins and all curses.

All the misery this world has witnessed — all its wars and bloodshed between nations, its selfishness and suffering, its ambitions and jealousies, its broken hearts and bitter lives, and all its everyday unhappiness — comes from what this cursed, hellish pride, our own or other people’s, has brought on us. It is pride that makes redemption necessary. It is from our pride that we need to be redeemed. How clearly we see our need of redemption will depend largely on how well we know the terrible nature of the power that has entered our being. The power Satan brought from hell and planted in human life is at work every day and every hour, with great strength, throughout the world. People suffer from it; they fear it, fight it and run from it; yet they do not recognise when it comes or when it has taken its terrible control.

No wonder, then, that they do not know where or how it can be overcome. Pride draws its root and strength from a terrible spiritual power that is outside us as well as within us. We must confess it and grieve over it as truly our own, but we also need to know it in its satanic origin. If that leads us to give up all hope of ever defeating it or driving it out, it will lead us all the sooner to the supernatural power in which alone our deliverance is found — the redemption of the Lamb of God. Our hopeless struggle against the workings of self and pride within us may feel even more hopeless when we think of the power of darkness behind it all. But that very despair will prepare us better to recognise and accept a power and a life outside ourselves as well: the humility of heaven, brought down and brought near by the Lamb of God to drive out Satan and his pride.

No tree can grow except from the root it sprang from. Just as we need to look at the first Adam and his fall to understand the power of the sin within us, we need to know the Second Adam well, and His power to give us a life of humility as real, as lasting and as overwhelming as our life of pride has been. We draw our life from Christ and live it in Christ just as truly as — no, more truly than — we drew it from Adam and lived it in him. We are to walk “rooted in Him,” holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body grows with the growth that comes from God.

The life of God, which entered human nature in the incarnation, is the root in which we are to stand and grow. The same almighty power that worked there, and on through to the resurrection, works in us every day. Our one need is to study, know and trust the life revealed in Christ as the life that is now ours — a life that waits only for our consent to take possession of our whole being and rule it.

That is why it is so enormously important to think rightly about who Christ is, about what really makes Him the Christ, and especially about what we can call His chief characteristic — the root and essence of His whole character as our Redeemer. There can be only one answer: His humility. What is the incarnation but His heavenly humility — His emptying Himself and becoming a man? What is His life on earth but humility — His taking the form of a servant? And what is His atonement but humility? “He humbled himself by becoming obedient” (Philippians 2:8). And what are His ascension and His glory but humility raised to the throne and crowned with glory? “Therefore God has highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:9). In heaven with the Father, in His birth, in His life, in His death and on His throne, it is all humility and nothing else.

Christ is the humility of God made flesh in human nature: eternal Love humbling itself and putting on the clothing of gentleness and kindness in order to win us, serve us and save us. Just as God’s love and willingness to stoop make Him the benefactor, helper and servant of all, so Jesus was necessarily Humility in human form. And so He still is, in the middle of the throne, the gentle and lowly Lamb of God. If this is the root of the tree, its nature must show in every branch, every leaf and every fruit.

If humility is the first grace in the life of Jesus, the one that includes all the others — if humility is the secret of His atonement — then the health and strength of our spiritual life will depend entirely on putting this grace first as well: making humility the chief thing we admire in Him, the chief thing we ask Him for, and the one thing for which we give up everything else. Is it any wonder that the Christian life is so often weak and fruitless, when the very root of Christ’s life is neglected and unknown? Is it any wonder that the joy of salvation is so seldom felt, when what Christ found and brings is so seldom looked for? We need a humility that is content with the end and death of self; that gives up all human praise, as Jesus did, to seek the honour that comes from God alone; that makes itself nothing and counts itself nothing, so that God may be everything and the Lord alone may be exalted. Until that is what we seek in Christ above every other joy, and welcome at any price, there is very little hope of a faith that will conquer the world.

I cannot urge my readers strongly enough: if your attention has never yet been drawn to how little humility there is in you or around you, stop and ask whether you see much of the spirit of the gentle and lowly Lamb of God in those who carry His name.

Consider all lack of love, all indifference to other people’s needs, feelings and weaknesses, and all the sharp, hasty judgments and remarks that are so often excused as simply being frank and honest.

All displays of temper, touchiness and irritation, and all feelings of bitterness and estrangement, are rooted in a pride that is always seeking itself. Your eyes will be opened to see how a dark, devilish pride creeps in almost everywhere — the gatherings of God’s people included. Begin to ask what would happen if, in you and around you, believers were truly and permanently guided by the humility of Jesus in their dealings with each other and with the world. Then say whether the cry of your whole heart, night and day, should not be: Oh, for the humility of Jesus in me and in everyone around me!

Fix your heart honestly on how much you lack the humility revealed in the pattern of Christ’s life and in the whole character of His redemption, and you will begin to feel that you have never really known what Christ and His salvation are. Believer, study the humility of Jesus. This is the secret, the hidden root, of your redemption. Sink deeper into it day by day.

Believe with your whole heart that this Christ whom God has given you — just as His divine humility did the work for you — will come in to live and work within you too, and make you what the Father wants you to be.

Note B. We need to know two things. The first is that our salvation consists entirely in being saved from ourselves — from what we are by nature. The second is that, in the whole nature of things, nothing could be this salvation or this saviour to us except a humility of God that is beyond all words.

Hence the Saviour’s first, unchangeable condition for fallen humanity: unless a man denies himself, he cannot be My disciple (Matthew 16:24). Self is the whole evil of fallen nature, and self-denial is what makes us capable of being saved. Humility is our saviour, while self is the root, the branches and the tree of all the evil of our fallen state. All the evils of fallen angels and fallen people are born from the pride of self. All the virtues of the heavenly life, on the other hand, are the virtues of humility.

It is humility alone that makes the great gulf between heaven and hell impassable.

What, then, is at stake in the great struggle for eternal life? Everything comes down to the battle between pride and humility. Pride and humility are the two ruling powers, the two kingdoms fighting for eternal possession of the human soul. There never has been, and never will be, more than one humility, and that is the humility of Christ. Pride and self are all that a person has until he receives everything from Christ. So the only one who fights the good fight is the one whose struggle is to see the self-worshipping nature he inherited from Adam put to death by the supernatural humility of Christ brought to life in him.

fields.title: Humility in the Life of Jesus
fields.body_html:
“But I am among you as the one who serves.” Luke 22:27.

In the Gospel of John, the inner life of our Lord is laid open to us. Jesus speaks often of His relationship to the Father, of the motives that guide Him, and of His awareness of the power and the spirit in which He acts. The word “humble” never appears there, yet nowhere in Scripture will we see so clearly what His humility consisted of. We have already said that this grace is really nothing but the creature’s simple consent to let God be everything — a consent by which it gives itself up to God’s working alone.

In Jesus we will see how, both as the Son of God in heaven and as a man on earth, He took a place of complete submission and gave God the honour and glory that are His due. And what He so often taught came true in His own life: “whoever humbles himself will be exalted.”

(Matthew 23:12). As it is written, “Therefore God has highly exalted Him” (Philippians 2:9).

Listen to the way our Lord speaks of His relationship to the Father, and notice how constantly He uses the words “not” and “nothing” about Himself. The “not I” with which Paul describes his relationship to Christ is exactly the spirit of what Christ says about His relationship to the Father.

“The Son can do nothing of his own accord” (John 5:19).

“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will.”

(John 5:30).

“I do not receive glory from people” (John 5:41).

“I have come down from heaven, not to do my own” (John 6:38).

“My teaching is not mine” (John 7:16). “I have not come of my own” (John 7:28). “I can do nothing on my own” (John 8:28). “I came not of my own accord, but he sent me” (John 8:42).

“I do not seek my own glory” (John 8:50). “The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority” (John 14:10).

“The word that you hear is not mine” (John 14:24).

These words open up the deepest roots of Christ’s life and work. They tell us how almighty God was able to do His mighty work of redemption through Him. They show what Christ considered the right condition of heart for Him as the Son of the Father. And they teach us the essential nature and life of the redemption Christ accomplished and now shares with us. It is this: He was nothing, so that God might be everything. He gave Himself up — His will and His powers — entirely to the Father, for the Father to work in Him. About His own power, His own will and His own glory, about His whole mission with all His works and all His teaching, He said: It is not I. I am nothing. I have given Myself to the Father to work. I am nothing; the Father is everything.

Christ found this life of complete self-denial, of total submission and dependence on the Father’s will, to be a life of perfect peace and joy. He lost nothing by giving everything to God. God honoured His trust, did everything for Him, and then raised Him to His own right hand in glory (Acts 5:31).

And because Christ had humbled Himself like this before God, and God was always before His eyes, He found He could humble Himself before people too, and be the Servant of all. His humility was simply the surrender of Himself to God, letting God do in Him whatever He pleased, no matter what the people around Him might say about Him or do to Him.

It is in this frame of mind, in this spirit and attitude, that Christ’s redemption has its power and effect. We are made sharers in Christ precisely to bring us into this attitude. This is the true self-denial our Saviour calls us to: admitting that self has nothing good in it except as an empty vessel for God to fill, and that its claim to be or to do anything must not be allowed for a moment. Being conformed to Jesus consists in this above and before everything else: being nothing and doing nothing of ourselves, so that God may be everything. Here we find the root and nature of true humility. It is because this is not understood or sought after that our humility is so shallow and so weak.

We must learn from Jesus, for He is gentle and lowly in heart. He teaches us that true humility begins, and finds its strength, in knowing that it is God who works everything in everyone; that our place is to yield to Him in complete surrender and dependence, fully consenting to be nothing and do nothing of ourselves. This is the life Christ came to reveal and to give — a life lived for God that comes through death to sin and to self. If this life seems too high and beyond our reach, then we must look for it in Him. It is Christ living within us who will live out this gentle and lowly life in us.

If we long for this, then above everything else let us seek the holy secret of knowing God’s nature — how He is at work every moment in everything. All of nature, every creature, and above all every child of God, is meant to bear witness to this secret: that each is nothing but a vessel, a channel, through which the living God can show the riches of His wisdom, power and goodness. The root of every virtue and grace, of all faith and of all worship that pleases God, is to know that we have nothing except what we receive, and to bow in the deepest humility and wait on God for it.

This humility was not a passing feeling in Jesus, stirred up and put into practice only when He thought about God. It was the very spirit of His whole life. That is why Jesus was just as humble in His dealings with people as He was with God. He saw Himself as God’s Servant for the people God had made and loved, and as a natural result He counted Himself the Servant of people, so that through Him God could do His work of love. Not for a moment did He think of seeking His own honour or using His power to defend Himself. His whole spirit was that of a life given over to God for God to work in.

Christians must study the humility of Jesus as the very heart of His redemption, as the very happiness of the life of the Son of God, as the only true relationship to the Father — and therefore as something Jesus must give us if we are to have any share with Him. Until they do, the terrible lack of real, heavenly, visible humility will not become a burden and a grief to them, and they will not set aside their ordinary religion to secure this, the first and chief mark of Christ within us.

Brother, sister, are you clothed with humility? Ask your daily life. Ask Jesus. Ask your friends.

Ask the world. And begin to praise God that in Jesus He has opened to you a heavenly humility you have hardly known — one through which a heavenly happiness you may never yet have tasted can come into your life.

fields.title: Humility in the Teaching of Jesus
fields.body_html:
“Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” Matthew 11:29. “And whoever would be first among you must be your slave, even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” Matthew 20:27.

We have seen humility in Christ’s life, as He opened His heart to us. Now let us listen to His teaching. There we will hear how He speaks about humility, and how far He expects people — and especially His disciples — to be humble as He was. Let us study the passages carefully (I can do little more than quote them), so that we take in the full impression of how often and how earnestly He taught it. That will help us grasp what He is asking of us.

Look at the beginning of His ministry. In the Beatitudes that open the Sermon on the Mount, He says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.” (Matthew 5:3, 5). The very first words of His announcement of the kingdom of heaven show us the open gate — the only one through which we can enter.

The kingdom comes to the poor, who have nothing in themselves.

The earth will belong to the meek, who seek nothing for themselves. The blessings of heaven and earth are for the lowly.

In heavenly life and in earthly life alike, humility is the secret of blessing.

“Learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” (Matthew 11:29). Jesus offers Himself as a Teacher. He tells us what spirit we will find in Him as our Teacher — the spirit we can learn from Him and receive from Him. Gentleness and lowliness are the one thing He offers us, and in them we will find perfect rest for our souls.

In the Gospels we see the disciples arguing about who would be the greatest in the kingdom, and they agreed to ask the Master (Luke 9:46, Matthew 18:3-5). He set a child in the middle of them and said, “Whoever humbles himself like this child, shall be exalted.” “Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” Matthew 18:1. It is a far-reaching question. What will be the chief distinction in the kingdom of heaven? No one but Jesus would have given the answer He gave: the chief glory of heaven, the truly heavenly mind, the greatest of the graces, is humility. “Whoever receives this child in my name receives me, and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.

For he who is least among you all is the great one.” Luke 9:48.

The sons of Zebedee had asked Jesus who would sit at His right and His left — the highest places in the kingdom. Jesus said those places were not His to give; they belonged to the Father, who would give them to those for whom they had been prepared. The disciples were not to look for them or ask for them. Their thoughts must be on the cup and the baptism of humiliation. Then He added, “Whoever would be first among you must be your slave, even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve” Matthew 20:27. Humility, as it is the mark of Christ the heavenly One, will be the one measure of glory in heaven. The lowliest is the one nearest to God.

First place in the Church is promised to the humblest. Speaking to the crowds and the disciples about the Pharisees and their love of the best seats, Christ said once again (Matthew 23:11), “The greatest among you shall be your servant.” Humbling ourselves is the only ladder to honour in God’s kingdom.

On another occasion, in a Pharisee’s house, He told the parable of the guest who is invited to move up to a better seat (Luke 14:1-11), and added, “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” Luke 14:11. The requirement cannot be bargained with; there is no other way. Only those who lower themselves will be lifted up.

After the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector, Christ said it again (Luke 18:14): “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” In the temple, in God’s presence and in His worship, everything is worthless unless it is filled with a deep, true humility towards God and towards people.

After washing the disciples’ feet, Jesus said (John 13:14), “If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” The authority of His command and of His example — every consideration of obedience or of becoming like Him — makes humility the first and most essential element of being a disciple. At the table of the Last Supper the disciples were still arguing about who was the greatest (Luke 22:26). Jesus said, “The greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves. I am among you as the one who serves.”

The path Jesus walked and opened up for us, the power and spirit in which He won our salvation, and the life He saves us into, is always the humility that makes me the servant of all. How little this is preached! How little it is practised! How little its absence is felt or confessed! I am not saying how few reach some recognisable measure of likeness to Jesus in His humility. I am saying how few ever think of making it a definite object of constant desire and prayer. How little the world has seen of it — and how little it has been seen even in the inner circle of the Church! “Let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves.” We all know what the character of a faithful servant involves: devotion to the master’s interests, careful thought about how to please him, and delight in his success, his honour and his happiness. There have been servants on earth in whom these qualities could be seen, and for whom the name “servant” was never anything but an honour.

For so many of us it has been a new joy in the Christian life to discover that we may give ourselves to God as servants, as slaves, and to find that serving Him is our highest freedom — freedom from sin and from self. Now we need to learn another lesson: Jesus calls us to be servants of one another, and as we accept that wholeheartedly, this service too will be deeply blessed, a new and fuller freedom from sin and self.

At first it may seem hard, but only because of the pride that still thinks it is something.

Once we learn that being nothing before God is the glory of the creature, the spirit of Jesus and the joy of heaven, we will welcome with our whole heart the training that comes from serving even people who try to irritate us. When our heart is set on this — on true holiness — we will study every word of Jesus about lowering ourselves with fresh eagerness. No place will be too low, no stooping too deep, no service too humble or too long, if only we can share and prove our fellowship with Him who said, “I am among you as the one who serves.” (Luke 22:27).

Friends, here is the path to the higher life. Down — lower down! That is what Jesus always said to disciples who were thinking about being great in the kingdom and sitting at His right hand and His left. Do not look for exaltation or ask for it; that is God’s work. Your work is to make sure you humble yourselves and take no place before God or people except that of a servant. Let that be your one aim and prayer. God is faithful. Just as water always seeks and fills the lowest place, so the moment God finds a creature humbled and empty, His glory and power flow in to lift it up and bless it. “He who humbles himself” — that must be our one concern — “will be exalted” — that is God’s concern, and by His mighty power and in His great love He will do it.

People sometimes talk as if humility and gentleness would rob us of what is noble, bold and strong. If only everyone would believe that this is the true nobility of the kingdom of heaven, that this is the royal spirit the King of heaven showed, that this is what it means to be like God — to humble oneself and become the servant of all! This is the path to the gladness and glory of Christ’s presence always in us and His power always resting on us. Jesus, the gentle and lowly One, calls us to learn from Him the way to God.

Let us study the words we have been reading until our hearts are filled with one thought: my one need is humility. And let us believe that what He shows us, He gives us; what He is, He shares with us. As the gentle and lowly One, He will come in and live in the heart that longs for Him.

fields.title: Humility in the Disciples of Jesus
fields.body_html:
“Let the greatest among you become as the youngest, and the leader as one who serves.” Luke 22:26.

We have studied humility in the person and the teaching of Jesus. Now let us look for it among the companions He chose, the twelve apostles. If the lack of it we find in them makes the contrast between Christ and ordinary people stand out more clearly, it will help us appreciate the mighty change Pentecost brought about in them. It will also show how real our own share can be in the complete triumph of Christ’s humility over the pride Satan breathed into humanity. In the passages we have quoted from Jesus’ teaching, we have already seen the occasions when the disciples showed how completely they lacked the grace of humility. Once they had been arguing on the road about which of them would be the greatest.

Another time, the sons of Zebedee and their mother asked for the first places — the seats at His right hand and His left. And later, at the supper table on the last night, there was another quarrel about which of them should be counted the greatest. In His ascension He received the Spirit of the Father. Through the Spirit He could do what He could not do while on earth: make Himself one with those He loved and live their life for them, so that they could live before the Father in a humility like His — because it was He Himself who lived and breathed in them. Others can joyfully testify to spiritual blessing and power, and yet have never been convinced of what the people around them can still see is missing. And still others can testify that the Lord has given them deliverance and victory in this grace, even as He has taught them how much more they still need and may expect from the fullness of Jesus.

fields.title: Humility in Daily Life
fields.body_html:
“If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar; for he who does not love his brother whom he has seen cannot love God whom he has not seen.” 1 John 4:20.

What a sobering thought: our love for God will be measured by our everyday dealings with people and the love they show. Our love for God will turn out to be an illusion unless it proves true by standing the test of daily life with those around us. It is exactly the same with our humility. It is easy to think we humble ourselves before God, but humility towards people is the only adequate proof that our humility before God is real. It shows that humility has made its home in us and become our very nature — that, like Christ, we have truly made ourselves of no reputation. When, in the presence of God, lowliness of heart has become not just a posture we take up in prayer but the very spirit of our life, it will show itself in the whole way we treat our brothers and sisters.

This is a lesson of great importance. The only humility that is really ours is not the humility we try to show God in prayer, but the humility we carry with us and live out in our ordinary behaviour.

The small, insignificant things of daily life carry the weight of eternity and are its tests, because they prove what spirit really possesses us. It is in our most unguarded moments that we truly show, and see, what we are.

To know a humble person — to know how a humble person behaves — you must follow them through the ordinary course of daily life. Isn’t this what Jesus taught? He gave His lessons on humility when the disciples were arguing about who should be the greatest, when He saw how the Pharisees loved the best places at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues, and when He had given them the example of washing their feet.

Humility before God is nothing unless it is proved by humility before people. Paul teaches the same thing. To the Romans he writes: “Outdo one another in showing honor.” (Romans 12:10); “Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be wise in your own sight.” Romans 12:16.

“Be not wise in your own eyes” Proverbs 3:7. To the Corinthians: “Love” — and there is no love without humility as its root — “does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud.” 1 Corinthians 13:4.

To the Galatians: “Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.” To the Ephesians, immediately after the three wonderful chapters on the heavenly life: “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love”; “Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ.”

To the Philippians: “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.” Philippians 2:3. “Have this mind among yourselves, which is yours in Christ Jesus.” Philippians 2:5. “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” Philippians 2:7.

To the Colossians: “Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you” Colossians 3:12-13.

It is in our relationships with one another, in the way we treat one another, that true lowliness of mind and a humble heart can be seen. Our humility before God has no value except as it prepares us to show the humility of Jesus to the people around us. Let us study humility in daily life in the light of these words.

The humble person tries at all times to live by the rule, “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves.” Philippians 2:3. People often ask: how can we count others better than ourselves when we can see that they are far below us in wisdom and holiness, in natural gifts, or in the grace they have received? The very question shows how little we understand what real lowliness of mind is.

True humility comes when, in the light of God, we have seen ourselves to be nothing and have agreed to let go of self and throw it away, so that God may be everything. The soul that has done this, and can say, “I have lost myself in finding You,” no longer compares itself with others. It has given up for ever every thought of self in God’s presence. It meets other people as one who is nothing and seeks nothing for itself. It is a servant of God, and for His sake a servant of all.

A faithful servant may be wiser than his master and still keep the true spirit and posture of a servant. The humble person looks on every child of God — even the weakest and least worthy — and honours them and gives them first place, as children of a King. The spirit of the One who washed the disciples’ feet makes it a joy for us to be truly the least, to be servants of one another. The humble person feels no jealousy or envy. He can praise God when others are preferred and blessed ahead of him.

He can bear to hear others praised and himself forgotten, because in God’s presence he has learned to say with Paul, “I am nothing.” He has received, as the spirit of his life, the spirit of Jesus, who did not please Himself and did not seek His own honour. The failings and sins of fellow Christians bring what are counted as temptations to impatience and touchiness, to hard thoughts and sharp words. In the middle of them, the humble person carries this often-repeated command in his heart and shows it in his life: “bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you.” He has learned that in putting on the Lord Jesus he has put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience.

Jesus has taken the place of self, and so it is possible to forgive as Jesus forgave. This humility does not consist only in thoughts or words that run oneself down. As Paul puts it, it is “a heart of humility,” surrounded by compassion and kindness, gentleness and patience — the sweet and lowly gentleness recognised as the mark of the Lamb of God.

In reaching for the deeper experiences of the Christian life, believers are often in danger of aiming at, and taking pleasure in, what we might call the more human, “manly” virtues: boldness, joy, contempt for the world, zeal and self-sacrifice. Even the ancient Stoics taught and practised these.

Meanwhile the deeper and gentler graces — the more divine and heavenly ones, which Jesus was the first to teach on earth because He brought them from heaven, and which are more closely tied to His cross and to the death of self: poverty of spirit, gentleness, humility, lowliness — are hardly thought about or valued. So let us put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. And let us prove that we are like Christ not only by our zeal to save the lost, but above all in the way we treat our fellow believers, bearing with one another and forgiving one another, just as the Lord forgave us.

Fellow Christians, let us study the Bible’s portrait of the humble person. And let us ask our brothers and sisters, and the world, whether they recognise in us a likeness to that original. Let us be satisfied with nothing less than taking each of these verses as a promise of what God will do in us — a revelation in words of what the Spirit of Jesus will bring to birth within us. And let every failure and shortcoming simply drive us to turn humbly and gently to the gentle and lowly Lamb of God, confident that where He is enthroned in the heart, His humility and gentleness will be one of the streams of living water flowing from within us.

“I knew Jesus, and He was very precious to my soul, but I found something in me that would not keep sweet, patient, and kind. I did what I could to keep it down, but it was there. I besought Jesus to do something for me, and when I gave Him my will, He came to my heart, and took out all that would not be sweet, kind, and patient, and then He shut the door.” George Foxe.

I repeat what I have said before. I feel deeply that we have very little idea how much the Church suffers from the lack of divine humility — the nothingness that makes room for God to show His power. Not long ago a Christian with a humble, loving spirit, who knew a good number of mission stations run by various societies, told me of his deep sorrow that in some of them the spirit of love and patience was sadly missing. Men and women who at home could each choose their own circle of friends were now thrown closely together with people they did not naturally get on with. They found it hard to bear with them, to love them, and to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. People who should have been helping each other’s joy became a hindrance and a burden to one another. The reason is the lack of a humility that counts itself nothing, that is glad to become and be counted the least, and that seeks only, like Jesus, to be the servant, helper and comforter of others — even the lowest and least worthy.

And why is it that people who have gladly given themselves up for Christ find it so hard to give themselves up for their brothers and sisters? Is the Church not to blame? It has taught its children so little that the humility of Christ is the first of the virtues, the best of all the graces and powers of the Spirit.

The Church has done so little to show that a Christlike humility is what it, like Christ, puts first and preaches first — as something truly needed, and something truly possible. But let us not be discouraged. Let the discovery that we lack this grace stir us to expect more from God. Let us look on every brother or sister who tests or irritates us as God’s means of grace — His instrument for purifying us and for exercising the humility that Jesus, our Life, breathes into us. And let us have such faith in God being everything and self being nothing that, as nothing in our own eyes, we may seek in God’s power only to serve one another in love.

fields.title: Humility and Holiness
fields.body_html:
“Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.” Isaiah 65:5.

We talk about the holiness movement of our day, and we praise God for it. We hear a great deal about people seeking holiness and people professing it, about holiness teaching and holiness meetings. The wonderful truths of holiness in Christ, and of holiness by faith, are being emphasised as never before. The great test of whether the holiness we claim to have reached is true and alive will be whether it shows itself in the growing humility it produces. For a creature, humility is the one thing needed to let God’s holiness live in it and shine through it. In Jesus, the Holy One of God who makes us holy, a divine humility was the secret of His life, His death and His exaltation. So the one sure test of our holiness will be the humility before God and people that marks our lives. Humility is the flower and the beauty of holiness.

The chief mark of counterfeit holiness is its lack of humility. Everyone who seeks holiness needs to be on guard, in case what began in the Spirit is unknowingly finished in the flesh, and pride creeps in where it is least expected. Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. There is no place or position so sacred that the Pharisee cannot get in. Pride can raise its head in the very temple of God and turn His worship into a stage for its own self-exaltation.

Ever since Christ exposed his pride so clearly, the Pharisee has put on the clothes of the tax collector. The person who confesses deep sinfulness must be just as watchful as the person who professes the highest holiness. Just when we most want our hearts to be in God’s temple, we will find the two men coming up to pray. And the tax collector will find that his danger does not come from the Pharisee beside him, who despises him, but from the Pharisee inside him, who praises and exalts him.

In God’s temple, when we think we are in the Most Holy Place, in the presence of His holiness, let us beware of pride. “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.” Job 1:6. “God, I thank you that I am not like other men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.” Luke 18:11. Self can find its reason for self-satisfaction in the very thing that is a real cause for thanksgiving — in the very thanks we give to God, even in the very confession that God has done it all. Yes, even in the temple, where the language of repentance and of trust in God’s mercy alone is heard, the Pharisee can take up the song of praise and, while thanking God, be congratulating himself.

Pride can dress itself in the clothes of praise or of repentance. Even when the words “I am not like other men” are rejected and condemned, their spirit can too often be found in the way we feel and speak about our fellow worshippers and fellow human beings. If you want to know whether this is really so, just listen to how churches and Christians often talk about one another. How little of the gentleness and kindness of Jesus can be seen!

It is so seldom remembered that deep humility must be the keynote of everything the servants of Jesus say about themselves or each other. Isn’t there many a church or gathering of believers, many a mission or conference, many a society or committee, even many a mission station far overseas, where harmony has been disturbed and God’s work held back? People counted as saints have shown, by touchiness, haste, impatience, self-defence, self-assertion, harsh judgments and unkind words, that they did not each regard others as better than themselves, and that their holiness had very little of the gentleness of the saints in it.

In their spiritual history, people may have had seasons of deep humbling and brokenness. But that is different from being clothed with humility, from having a humble spirit, from having the lowliness of mind in which each one counts himself the servant of others and so shows the very mind that was in Christ Jesus. “Do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.” Isaiah 65:5. What a parody of holiness! Jesus the Holy One is the humble One; the holiest will always be the humblest. No one is holy but God, so we have exactly as much holiness as we have of God.

Our real humility is the measure of how much of God we have, because humility is nothing but self disappearing in the vision that God is everything. The holiest will be the humblest. Sadly, though the openly boasting Israelite of Isaiah’s day is seldom found now — good manners have taught us not to talk like that — his spirit is still often seen, whether in the way we treat fellow believers or the people of the world.

In the spirit in which opinions are given, work is taken on and faults are pointed out, how often the clothes are the tax collector’s but the voice is still the Pharisee’s: “God, I thank you that I am not like other men.” Is there a humility to be found in which people truly count themselves less than the least of all the saints, the servants of all? There is. “love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant” (1 Corinthians 13:4) — and that love is found where the spirit of love has been poured into the heart, where the divine nature comes to full birth, where Christ the gentle and lowly Lamb of God is truly formed within.

There is the power of a perfect love that forgets itself and finds its happiness in blessing others, in bearing with them and honouring them, however weak they are. Where this love comes in, God comes in. And where God has come in His power and shows Himself to be everything, the creature becomes nothing. Where the creature has become nothing before God, it cannot be anything but humble towards its fellow creatures. The presence of God is no longer something for special times and seasons; it becomes the shelter under which the soul always lives, and its deep humbling before God becomes the holy place of His presence from which all its words and actions come.

May God teach us that our thoughts, words and feelings about other people are His test of our humility towards Him, and that our humility before Him is the only power that can keep us humble with others. Our humility must be the life of Christ, the Lamb of God, within us.

Let every teacher of holiness, in the pulpit or on the platform, and every seeker after holiness, in the prayer room or at the conference, take warning. There is no pride as dangerous as the pride of holiness, because none is so subtle and so sly. It is not that anyone ever says, or even thinks, “Do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.” Isaiah 65:5. No — that thought would be regarded with horror. But without our noticing, a hidden habit of the soul grows up that is quietly pleased with its achievements and cannot help seeing how far ahead of others it is.

It can be recognised not always by any particular self-assertion or self-praise, but simply by the absence of the deep self-humbling that is bound to mark a soul that has seen the glory of God (Job 42:5-6; Isaiah 6:5). It shows itself not only in words or thoughts, but in a tone — a way of speaking about others in which those with spiritual discernment cannot help recognising the power of self. Even the world, with its sharp eyes, notices it and points to it as proof that claiming a heavenly life does not produce any particularly heavenly fruit.

Friends, let us beware! Unless every step forward in what we think of as holiness is matched by a deeper study of humility, we may discover that we have been enjoying beautiful thoughts and feelings, solemn acts of consecration and faith, while the only sure sign of God’s presence — the disappearance of self — was missing all along. Come, let us run to Jesus and hide ourselves in Him until we are clothed with His humility.

That alone is our holiness.

fields.title: Humility and Sin
fields.body_html:
“Sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” 1 Timothy 1:15. Humility is often equated with repentance and sorrow for sin. As a result, it seems that the only way to grow in humility is to keep the soul focused on its sin. We have learned that humility is something more. We have seen in the teaching of our Lord Jesus and in the letters of the apostles how often this virtue is urged with no reference to sin at all. In the very nature of things — in the whole relationship of the creature to the Creator, and in the life of Jesus as He lived it and shares it with us — humility is the very essence of holiness and happiness. It is self being displaced as God is enthroned, so that God is everything and self is nothing.

That side of the truth is the one I have felt it especially necessary to press. But now we must see the new depth and intensity that sin, and God’s grace, give to the humility of the saints. We only need to look at someone like the apostle Paul to see how, all through his life as a redeemed and holy man, the deep awareness of having been a sinner stayed alive and could not be put out. We all know the passages where he refers to his life as a persecutor and blasphemer.

“I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God… I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.” (1 Corinthians 15:9-10). “To me, though I am the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ” (Ephesians 3:8). “Though formerly I was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent. But I received mercy because I had acted ignorantly in unbelief… Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” (1 Timothy 1:13, 15). God’s grace had saved him.

God would never again remember his sins — but Paul could never forget how terribly he had sinned.

The more he rejoiced in God’s salvation, and the more his experience of God’s grace filled him with joy beyond words, the clearer his awareness became that he was a saved sinner, and that salvation had no meaning or sweetness except as the sense of being a sinner made it precious and real to him. Not for a moment could he forget that it was a sinner whom God had taken up in His arms and crowned with His love.

The passages we have just quoted are often cited as Paul’s confession of daily sin. You only have to read them carefully in context to see how far that is from the truth. Their meaning goes much deeper. They refer to something that lasts through all eternity, something that will give its deep undertone of wonder and worship to the humility with which the redeemed bow before the throne, as those who have been washed from their sins in the blood of the Lamb. Even in glory they can never be anything other than redeemed sinners. And never, for a single moment in this life, can God’s child live in the full light of His love except by feeling that the sin he has been saved from is his one and only claim to everything grace has promised to do.

The humility with which he first came as a sinner takes on a new meaning when he learns how fitting it is for him as a creature. And then, again and again, the humility he was born into as a creature finds its deepest, richest notes of worship in the memory of what it means to be a monument to God’s wonderful redeeming love. The full force of what Paul’s words teach us comes out strongly when we notice a remarkable fact. Through his whole Christian life, we never find anything from his pen that resembles a confession of sin — not even in the letters where he opens his heart most personally. Nowhere does he mention any shortcoming or failing; nowhere does he suggest to his readers that he has failed in his duty or sinned against the law of perfect love.

On the contrary, there are quite a few passages where he defends himself in words that mean nothing unless they appeal to a blameless life before God and people. “You are witnesses, and God also, how holy and righteous and blameless was our conduct toward you believers.” (1 Thessalonians 2:10). “For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.” (2 Corinthians 1:12).

This is not an ideal or a goal; it is an appeal to what his life had actually been. However we explain the absence of any confession of sin, everyone will agree that it points to a life lived in the power of the Holy Spirit of a kind that is seldom experienced, or even expected, today. My point is this: the absence of such confessions only makes it clearer that the secret of deeper humility is not found in daily sinning. It is found in a settled position, never to be forgotten for a moment — one that more abundant grace only keeps more vividly alive. Our only place, the only place of blessing, our one lasting position before God, must be that of people whose highest joy is to confess that they are sinners saved by grace.

Paul’s deep memory of having sinned so terribly in the past, before grace met him, and his awareness of being kept from sinning now, always went together with a lasting awareness of the dark, hidden power of sin, always ready to come in and kept out only by the presence and power of Christ living within him.

“For I know that nothing good dwells in me” — these words of Romans 7:18 describe the flesh as it remains to the very end. The glorious deliverance of Romans 8:2, “For the law of the Spirit of life has set you free in Christ Jesus from the law of sin and death,” is neither the destruction of the flesh nor the making holy of the flesh. It is a continuous victory given by the Spirit as He puts to death the deeds of the body. As health drives out disease, as light swallows up darkness and as life conquers death, so Christ living in us through the Spirit is the health, light and life of the soul.

Alongside this, the conviction of our helplessness and danger always tempers our faith in the moment-by-moment, unbroken working of the Holy Spirit, producing that chastened sense of dependence that makes the highest faith and joy into servants of a humility that lives only by the grace of God. All three passages quoted above show that what humbled Paul so deeply was the wonderful grace given to him — grace he felt he needed every moment. It was the grace of God that was with him and enabled him to work harder than all the others; the grace to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ; the grace that overflowed with the faith and love found in Christ Jesus. It is the very nature and glory of this grace that it is for sinners, and it was this grace that kept so intensely alive his awareness that he had once sinned and could still sin.

“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” Romans 5:20. This shows that the very essence of grace is to deal with sin and take it away, and that the more abundant our experience of grace, the deeper our awareness of being sinners must be. It is not sin but God’s grace — showing a person, and constantly reminding him, what a sinner he was — that will keep him truly humble. It is not sin but grace that will make me really know myself as a sinner, and make the sinner’s place of deepest self-humbling the place I never leave.

I fear there are quite a few people who have tried to humble themselves through strong words of self-condemnation and self-accusation, and who must admit with sorrow that a humble spirit — “a heart of humility,” with the kindness and compassion, gentleness and patience that go with it — is as far away as ever. Being absorbed with self, even in the deepest self-loathing, can never free us from self. What will make us humble is the revelation of God — not only through the law, which condemns sin, but through His grace, which delivers from it.

The law may break the heart with fear; only grace produces the sweet humility that becomes a joy to the soul, a second nature. It was the revelation of God in His holiness, coming near to make Himself known in His grace, that made Abraham and Jacob, Job and Isaiah, bow so low. The soul that waits on God, trusts Him and worships Him — God the Creator as everything to the creature in its nothingness, and God the Redeemer in His grace as everything to the sinner in his sinfulness — will find itself so filled with His presence that there is no room left for self.

Only in this way can the promise be fulfilled: “And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.” Isaiah 2:17.

The sinner who lives in the full light of God’s holy, redeeming love — in the experience of that full indwelling of divine love that comes through Christ and the Holy Spirit — cannot help but be humble. Deliverance from self comes not from being absorbed with your sin, but from being absorbed with God.

fields.title: Humility and Faith
fields.body_html:
“How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” John 5:44.

In a talk I heard recently, the speaker said that the blessings of the deeper Christian life are often like goods displayed in a shop window: you can see them clearly, but you cannot reach them. Tell someone to stretch out his hand and take them, and he would answer, “I can’t. There is a thick sheet of glass between me and them.” In the same way, Christians may clearly see God’s wonderful promises of perfect peace and rest, of overflowing love and joy, of lasting fellowship with Him and fruitfulness, and yet feel that something stands in the way of really possessing them. The promises made to faith are so free and certain, the invitations and encouragements so strong, and God’s mighty power, on which faith can rely, so near and so freely given — so the only thing that can stop faith from taking hold and the blessing from becoming ours is pride.

In this verse Jesus shows us that it really is pride that makes faith impossible. John 5:44 says: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another?” As we see how pride and faith are, by their very nature, completely opposed, we will learn that faith and humility share one root, and that we can never have more true faith than we have true humility. We will see that a person can have strong intellectual conviction and certainty about the truth while still keeping pride in the heart — but pride makes living faith, the faith that has power with God, impossible.

We only need to think for a moment about what faith is. Isn’t it the admission that we are nothing and can do nothing — surrendering and waiting for God to work? Isn’t it, in itself, the most humbling thing there is: accepting our place as dependants who can claim, obtain or do nothing except what grace gives? Humility is the attitude that prepares the soul to live by trust. Even the faintest, most secret breath of pride — in self-seeking, self-will, self-confidence or self-exaltation — simply strengthens the self, and the self cannot enter or possess the things of the kingdom, because it refuses to let God be what He is and must be: everything in everything. Faith is the faculty, the sense, by which we perceive and grasp the heavenly world and its blessings. Faith seeks the glory that comes from God, and that glory comes only where God is everything.

As long as we accept glory from one another — as long as we seek, love and jealously guard the glory of this life, the honour and reputation people give — we are not seeking the glory that comes from God, and we cannot receive it. Pride makes faith impossible. Salvation comes through a cross and a crucified Christ. Salvation is fellowship with the crucified Christ in the spirit of His cross. Salvation is union with God and delight in God; salvation is sharing in the humility of Jesus. Is it any wonder our faith is so weak, when pride still rules so much in us, and we have barely learned even to long or pray for humility as the most necessary and most blessed part of salvation?

Humility and faith are more closely linked in Scripture than many people realise. See it in the life of Christ. There are two occasions on which He spoke of great faith. The centurion, whose faith amazed Him so that He said, “I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith,” had said, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.” And the mother to whom He said, “O woman, great is your faith!” (Matthew 15:28) had accepted being called a dog and answered, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs” (Matthew 15:27). The humility that brings a soul to be nothing before God also removes every obstacle to faith, so that its only fear is that it might dishonour Him by not trusting Him completely.

Friend, isn’t this the reason we have failed in our pursuit of holiness? Isn’t this what made our consecration and our faith so shallow and so short-lived, though we did not know it? We had no idea how much pride and self were still secretly at work in us, or that only God, by coming in with His mighty power, could drive them out. We didn’t understand that nothing but the new, divine nature, taking the place of the old self completely, could make us truly humble.

We did not know that complete, constant, all-embracing humility must be the root attitude of every prayer and every approach to God, as well as of every dealing with people. We did not know that we might as well try to see without eyes or live without breathing as try to believe, draw near to God or live in His love without a humility and lowliness of heart that runs through everything.

Friend, haven’t we been making a mistake — working so hard to believe, while all the time the old self, in its pride, was trying to take hold of God’s blessings and riches for itself? No wonder we could not believe. Let us change course. Let us first of all seek to humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God, and He will lift us up. The cross, death and the grave, into which Jesus humbled Himself, were His path to the glory of God.

Let our one desire and our earnest prayer be to be humbled with Him and like Him. Let us gladly accept whatever can humble us before God or people; this alone is the path to the glory of God. You may want to ask a question. I have mentioned people who have wonderful spiritual experiences, or who bring blessing to others, and yet lack humility. Don’t they prove, you ask, that they have true and even strong faith, even though they show all too clearly that they still seek far too much of the honour that comes from people? More than one answer could be given.

But the main answer, in our present context, is this: they do have a measure of faith, and the blessing they bring to others is in proportion to it, together with the special gifts they have been given.

But in that very blessing, the work of their faith is held back by their lack of humility. The blessing is often shallow or short-lived because they do not open the way for God to be everything. A deeper humility would certainly bring a deeper and fuller blessing. If the Holy Spirit not only worked in them as a Spirit of power but lived in them in the fullness of His grace — and especially the grace of humility — He would share Himself through them with their converts, giving them a life of power, holiness and steadfastness that is now seen far too seldom.

“How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another?” (John 5:44). Friend, nothing can cure you of the desire to receive glory from people — or of the touchiness, hurt and anger that come when it is not given — except giving yourself to seek only the glory that comes from God.

Let the glory of the all-glorious God be everything to you. You will be set free from the glory of people and of self, and be content and glad to be nothing. Out of that nothingness you will grow strong in faith, giving glory to God, and you will find that the deeper you sink in humility before Him, the closer He is to fulfilling every desire of your faith.
