fields.title: Humility and Death to Self
fields.body_html:
“He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death” Philippians 2:8.

Humility is the path to death, because it is in death that humility gives the highest proof of its perfection.

Humility is the blossom, and death to self is its perfect fruit. Jesus humbled Himself to the point of death and opened up the path we too must walk. There was no way for Him to prove His surrender to God to the very uttermost — no way to give up our human nature and rise out of it into the glory of the Father — except through death. It is the same for us.

Humility must lead us to die to self, and so prove how completely we have given ourselves up to it and to God. Only in this way are we set free from our fallen nature and find the path that leads to life in God — to the full birth of the new nature, whose breath and joy is humility. We have spoken of what Jesus did for His disciples when He shared His resurrection life with them. When the Holy Spirit came down, Jesus Himself — gentleness glorified and enthroned — actually came from heaven to live in them.

He won the power to do this through death. In its deepest nature, the life He gave them was a life out of death: a life that had been surrendered to death and won through death. The One who came to live in them was Himself the One who had been dead and is now alive for ever. Jesus’ life, His person and His presence bear the marks of death, the marks of a life born out of death. And that life in His disciples always bears the marks of death too. Only as the Spirit of His death — the Spirit of the One who died — lives and works in the soul can the power of His life be known.

The first and chief mark of the dying of the Lord Jesus — of the death marks that show who truly follows Him — is humility. There are two reasons for this: only humility leads to perfect death, and only death brings humility to perfection. Humility and death are one in their very nature. Humility is the bud; in death the fruit ripens to perfection.

Humility leads to perfect death. Humility means giving up self and taking the place of perfect nothingness before God. Jesus humbled Himself and became obedient to the point of death. In His death He gave the highest, most complete proof that He had given up His will to the will of God.

In death Jesus gave Himself up, together with His natural reluctance to drink the cup. He gave up the life He had in union with our human nature; He died to self and to the sin that tempted Him; and so, as a man, He entered the perfect life of God. Without His boundless humility, which counted Himself nothing except a servant to do and suffer the will of God, He would never have died. This answers a question that is often asked but whose meaning is seldom clearly understood: How can I die to self? Death to self is not your work; it is God’s work.

In Christ you are dead to sin. The life in you has gone through death and resurrection, and you can be sure that you really are dead to sin. But how fully the power of this death shows itself in your attitudes and behaviour depends on how fully the Holy Spirit gives you the power of Christ’s death. And this is where teaching is needed, if you want to enter into full fellowship with Christ in His death and know full deliverance from self: humble yourself. This is your one duty.

Put yourself before God in your complete helplessness. Agree wholeheartedly that you are powerless either to put yourself to death or to make yourself alive, and sink down into your own nothingness in a spirit of gentle, patient and trusting surrender to God. Accept every humiliation, and look on everyone who tests or irritates you as a means of grace to humble you. Use every opportunity of humbling yourself before other people as a help to staying humble before God.

God will accept this humbling of yourself as proof that your whole heart wants it — as the very best prayer for it, and as your preparation for His mighty work of grace. Then, by the powerful strengthening of His Holy Spirit, He will reveal Christ fully in you, so that Christ, in His form as a servant, is truly formed in you and lives in your heart. It is the path of humility that leads to perfect death — to the full and complete experience that we are dead in Christ.

And then it follows that only this death leads to perfect humility. Beware of the mistake so many people make: they would like to be humble, but they are afraid of being too humble. They have so many conditions and limits, so many arguments and questions about what true humility should be and do, that they never give themselves up to it without reserve. Beware of this. Humble yourself to the point of death. It is in dying to self that humility is made perfect. Be sure of this: at the root of every real experience of more grace, every true step forward in consecration and every growing likeness to Jesus, there must be a deadness to self that proves itself to God and to people in our attitudes and habits.

Sadly, it is possible to talk about the life that comes through death and the walk in the Spirit while even the tenderest love cannot help seeing how much self there still is. Death to self has no surer mark than a humility that makes itself of no reputation, that empties itself and takes the form of a servant. It is possible to speak a great deal, and sincerely, about fellowship with a despised and rejected Jesus and about carrying His cross, while the gentle and lowly, kind and tender humility of the Lamb of God is not seen and is hardly even sought.

The Lamb of God means two things: gentleness and death. Let us seek to receive Him in both. In Him they cannot be separated, so in us they must not be separated either. What a hopeless task it would be if we had to do the work ourselves! Nature can never overcome nature, not even with the help of grace. Self can never drive out self, even in someone who has been born again. Praise God, the work has been done, finished and made perfect for ever. The death of Jesus, once for all, is our death to self. And the ascension of Jesus — His entering once for all into the Most Holy Place — has given us the Holy Spirit to share with us in power, and make truly our own, the power of the life that comes through death.

As the soul follows in Jesus’ footsteps, pursuing and practising humility, it wakes up to its need of something more. Its desire and hope are stirred, its faith is strengthened, and it learns to look up, to claim and to receive the true fullness of the Spirit of Jesus — the Spirit who can keep His death to self and to sin working in full power day by day, and make humility the spirit that runs through our whole life. (See Note C at the end of this chapter.) Romans 6:3 says: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?”

Romans 6:11 says: “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus.” The Christian’s whole sense of who he is should be soaked in, and shaped by, the spirit that moved Christ in His death.

He must always present himself to God as someone who has died in Christ and in Christ is alive from the dead, carrying in his body the dying of the Lord Jesus. His life always bears this double mark: its roots go down in true humility deep into the grave of Jesus — death to sin and to self — while its head is lifted in resurrection power to heaven, where Jesus is.

Believer, claim by faith the death and the life of Jesus as yours. Enter His grave, into rest from self and its efforts — the rest of God. With Christ, who committed His spirit into the Father’s hands, humble yourself and go down each day into that perfect, helpless dependence on God.

God will raise you up and exalt you. Every morning, sink in deep, deep nothingness into the grave of Jesus, and every day the life of Jesus will be revealed in you.

Let a willing, loving, restful, happy humility be the sign that you have truly claimed your birthright — baptism into the death of Christ. “For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” Hebrews 10:14. Those who enter into His humiliation will find in Him the power to see self as dead and count it dead, and, as people who have learned from Him and received from Him, to walk with all lowliness and gentleness, bearing with one another in love. The life that comes through death is seen in a gentleness and lowliness like Christ’s.

Note C. To die to self — to come out from under its power — is not something we can do, and cannot be done, by any active resistance our natural powers can put up against it. The one true way of dying to self is the way of patience, gentleness, humility and surrender to God. This is the truth and the perfection of dying to self. If I ask you what the Lamb of God means, won’t you tell me that it is, and means, the perfection of patience, gentleness, humility and surrender to God? Then won’t you also have to say that desiring these virtues and believing for them is turning to Christ, giving yourself up to Him, and the perfection of faith in Him? And because this leaning of your heart to sink down in patience, gentleness, humility and surrender to God is truly giving up everything you are and everything you have from fallen Adam, it is perfectly leaving all you have to follow Christ. It is your highest act of faith in Him. Christ is nowhere but in these virtues; where they are, He is in His own kingdom. Let this be the Christ you follow.

“The Spirit of divine love can have no birth in any fallen creature until it wills and chooses to be dead to all self, in a patient, humble surrender to the power and mercy of God.” I seek my whole salvation through the merits and mediation of the gentle, humble, patient, suffering Lamb of God, who alone has the power to bring these heavenly virtues to birth in my soul. There is no possibility of salvation except in and through the birth of the gentle, humble, patient, surrendered Lamb of God in our souls.

When the Lamb of God has brought about a real birth of His own gentleness, humility and full surrender to God in our souls, that is the birthday of the Spirit of love in our souls. Whenever we reach it, it will feast our souls with such peace and joy in God that it will wipe out the memory of everything we called peace or joy before. “This way to God cannot fail. Its certainty rests on the twofold character of our Saviour:

1. As the Lamb of God, He is the source of all gentleness and humility in the soul.

2. As the Light of heaven, He blesses eternal nature and turns it into a kingdom of heaven. When we are willing to find rest for our souls in gentle, humble surrender to God, then He, as the Light of God and of heaven, joyfully breaks in on us, turns our darkness into light, and begins within us that kingdom of God and of love which will never end.”

See Wholly for God. (The whole passage deserves careful study. It shows most remarkably how continually sinking down in humility before God is, on our side, the only way to die to self.)

If I ask you what the Lamb of God means, won’t you tell me that it is, and means, the perfection of patience, gentleness, humility and surrender to God? Then won’t you also have to say that desiring these virtues and believing for them is turning to Christ, giving yourself up to Him, and the perfection of faith in Him? And because this leaning of your heart to sink down in patience, gentleness, humility and surrender to God is truly giving up everything you are and everything you have from fallen Adam, it is perfectly leaving all you have to follow Christ. fields.title: Humility and Happiness
fields.body_html:
“I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.” 2 Corinthians 12:9-10.

So that Paul would not become proud because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations he had received, a thorn in the flesh was sent to keep him humble. Paul’s first wish was to have it removed, and three times he begged the Lord to take it away. The answer came that the trial was a blessing: in the weakness and humiliation it brought, the Lord’s grace and strength could be shown more clearly. Paul immediately entered a new stage in his relationship to the trial. Instead of simply putting up with it, he gladly boasted in it. Instead of asking to be rescued from it, he took pleasure in it.

He had learned that the place of humiliation is the place of blessing, power and joy. Practically every Christian passes through these same two stages in the pursuit of humility. In the first, he fears and runs from everything that could humble him, and looks for a way out. He has not yet learned to seek humility at any cost. He has accepted the command to be humble and tries to obey it, only to discover how completely he fails. He prays for humility, sometimes very earnestly — but in his secret heart he prays even more, if not in words then in his wishes, to be spared the very things that would make him humble.

He is not yet so in love with humility — as the beauty of the Lamb of God and the joy of heaven — that he would sell everything to get it. In his pursuit of it and his prayers for it there is still a sense of burden and bondage. Humbling himself has not yet become the natural expression of a life and nature that is humble at its core. It has not yet become his joy and his only pleasure. He cannot yet say, “I most gladly boast in weakness; I take pleasure in whatever humbles me.” Can we hope to reach the stage where that is true? Certainly.

And what will bring us there? What brought Paul there: a new revelation of the Lord Jesus. Nothing but the presence of God can expose self and drive it out. Paul was to be given a clearer insight into a deep truth: the presence of Jesus will banish every desire to look for anything in ourselves, and will make us delight in every humiliation that prepares us for a fuller revelation of Him. As we experience the presence and power of Jesus, our humiliations lead us to choose humility as our highest blessing.

Let us try to learn the lessons Paul’s story teaches us. There can be mature believers, distinguished teachers and people of heavenly experiences who have not yet fully learned the lesson of perfect humility — of gladly boasting in weakness. We see this in Paul. The danger of becoming proud had come very close. He did not yet fully know what it meant to be nothing, to die so that Christ alone might live in him, and to take pleasure in everything that brought him low. It seems this was the highest lesson he had to learn: to be fully conformed to his Lord in that self-emptying in which he boasted in weakness so that God might be everything.

The highest lesson a believer has to learn is humility. Let every Christian who seeks to grow in holiness remember this well! There may be intense consecration, burning zeal and heavenly experience, and yet, unless the Lord prevents it by very special dealings, an unconscious self-exaltation may come along with it all.

Let us learn that the highest holiness is the deepest humility. And let us remember that it does not come by itself, but only as our faithful Lord makes it a matter of special dealing with His faithful servant. Let us look at our lives in the light of Paul’s experience and see whether we gladly boast in weakness — whether we take pleasure, as Paul did, in insults, in hardships and in times of distress.

Yes, let us ask whether we have learned to see a rebuke, fair or unfair; a reproach from friend or enemy; an injury, or a trouble or difficulty others bring us into — above all as an opportunity to prove that Jesus is everything to us, that our own pleasure and honour are nothing, and that humiliation is truly what we take pleasure in. It is a blessed thing, the deep happiness of heaven, to be so free from self that whatever is said about us or done to us is lost and swallowed up in the thought that Jesus is everything.

Let us trust the One who took charge of Paul to take charge of us too. Paul needed special discipline, and special instruction with it, to learn something more precious even than the inexpressible things he had heard in heaven: what it means to boast in weakness and lowliness. We need it too — oh, so much.

The One who cared for him will care for us as well. He watches over us with jealous, loving care, so that we do not become proud. When we start to, He works to show us the evil and to rescue us from it.

Through trials, weakness and trouble, He works to bring us low, until we learn so deeply that His grace is everything that we take pleasure in the very things that bring us low and keep us there. His strength made perfect in our weakness, His presence filling and satisfying our emptiness, becomes the secret of a humility that need never fail. Like Paul, such a soul can look fully at what God does in it and through it, and still say, “I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing.” 2 Corinthians 12:11.

His humiliations had led him to true humility, with its wonderful gladness and its boasting in everything that humbles.

“I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.” 2 Corinthians 12:9-10. The humble person has learned the secret of lasting gladness. The weaker he feels and the lower he sinks, the greater his humiliations seem, the more the power and presence of Christ become his portion — until, as he says, “I am nothing,” his Lord’s word brings ever deeper joy: “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). I feel I must gather everything up once more into two lessons: the danger of pride is greater and nearer than we think — and so is the grace for humility. The danger of pride is greater and nearer than we think, especially at the times of our highest experiences.

The preacher of spiritual truth with an admiring congregation hanging on his every word; the gifted speaker on a holiness platform explaining the secrets of the heavenly life; the Christian testifying to a wonderful experience; the evangelist moving on as if in triumph, a blessing to rejoicing crowds — no one knows the hidden, unconscious danger these people are exposed to. Paul was in danger without knowing it. What Jesus did for him is written as a warning for us, so that we may know our danger and know our only safety.

If it has ever been said of a teacher or professor of holiness, “He is so full of self,” or “He doesn’t practise what he preaches,” or “His blessing hasn’t made him any humbler or gentler,” let it never be said again. Jesus, in whom we trust, can make us humble. Yes, the grace for humility is also greater and nearer than we think. The humility of Jesus is our salvation. Jesus Himself is our humility.

Our humility is His concern and His work. His grace is sufficient for us, to meet the temptation of pride as well. His strength will be made perfect in our weakness. Let us choose to be weak, to be low and to be nothing.

Let humility be our joy and gladness. Let us gladly boast and take pleasure in weakness, in everything that can humble us and keep us low, so that the power of Christ will rest on us. Christ humbled Himself, and so God exalted Him. Christ will humble us and keep us humble. Let us consent with all our hearts and accept, trustingly and joyfully, everything that humbles us, and the power of Christ will rest on us.

We will find that the deepest humility is the secret of the truest happiness — a joy that nothing can destroy.

fields.title: Humility and Exaltation
fields.body_html:
“He who humbles himself will be exalted.” Luke 14:11, 18:14.

“Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.” James 4:10.

“Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you” 1 Peter 5:6.

Only yesterday someone asked me, “How am I to conquer this pride?” The answer was simple.

Two things are needed. Do what God says is your work: humble yourself. And trust Him to do what He says is His work: He will exalt you. The command is clear — humble yourself. That does not mean it is your job to conquer and drive out the pride of your nature and to form within yourself the lowliness of the holy Jesus. No, that is God’s work. It is the very heart of the exaltation in which He lifts you up into the real likeness of His beloved Son.

What the command means is this: take every opportunity to humble yourself before God and before people. Trust the grace that is already at work in you, and be sure of more grace for the victory that is coming. Respond to the light your conscience shines, again and again, on the pride of your heart and its workings. And in spite of all your failures and falls, keep standing, persistently, under the unchanging command: humble yourself.

Accept with gratitude everything God allows — from within or from outside, from friend or enemy, in nature or in grace — to remind you of your need to be humbled and to help you towards it. Count humility as truly the mother of all virtues, your very first duty before God, the one constant safeguard of the soul, and set your heart on it as the source of all blessing. The promise is divine and certain: whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). Make sure you do the one thing God asks: humble yourself. God will do the one thing He has promised: He will give you more grace, and He will exalt you at the right time.

All of God’s dealings with people follow two stages. First comes a time of preparation. Commands and promises, mixed with experiences of effort and helplessness, of failure and partial success, together with a holy expectation of something better, awaken people, train them and discipline them for a higher stage. Then comes the time of fulfilment, when faith inherits the promise and enjoys what it had so often struggled for in vain. This law holds true in every part of the Christian life and in the pursuit of every single virtue, because it is rooted in the very nature of things. In everything to do with our redemption, God must take the first step.

When He has done that, it is our turn. In striving to obey and to attain, we must come to know our helplessness, die to ourselves in self-despair, and so be made ready to receive from God — freely and with understanding — the completion of what we had accepted the beginning of without understanding. So God, who was the Beginning before we properly knew Him or fully understood His purpose, is longed for and welcomed as the End, as everything in everything. It is exactly the same in the pursuit of humility.

To every Christian the command comes from the throne of God Himself: humble yourself. An earnest attempt to listen and obey will be rewarded — rewarded, yes, with the painful discovery of two things. The first is how deep our pride goes: an unwillingness to count ourselves nothing, to be counted nothing, and to submit completely to God, deeper than we ever knew. The second is how utterly powerless all our efforts are — and all our prayers for God’s help, too — to destroy that ugly monster.

Blessed is the person who now learns to put his hope in God and to keep going, in spite of all the power of the pride within him, in acts of humbling himself before God and people. We know the law of human nature: actions produce habits, habits produce dispositions, dispositions shape the will, and a rightly shaped will is character.

It is no different in the work of grace. As actions, persistently repeated, produce habits and dispositions, and these strengthen the will, the One who works in us both to will and to act comes with His mighty power and Spirit. The repentant believer has thrown his proud heart down before God again and again, humbling it; that is rewarded with more grace — the grace of a humble heart, in which the Spirit of Jesus has conquered and brought the new nature to maturity, and in which He, the gentle and lowly One, now lives for ever. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will exalt you. And what does this exaltation consist of? The highest glory of the creature is simply to be a vessel that receives, enjoys and displays the glory of God.

It can do this only if it is willing to be nothing in itself, so that God may be everything. Water always fills the lowest places first. The lower and emptier a person lies before God, the faster and fuller the divine glory will flow in. The exaltation God promises is not, and cannot be, some outward thing separate from Himself. All He has to give, all He can give, is more of Himself — Himself taking more complete possession of us. This exaltation is not like an earthly prize, chosen arbitrarily and with no necessary link to the behaviour being rewarded. No — by its very nature it is the effect and result of our humbling ourselves. It is nothing other than the gift of a divine humility living within us — such likeness to, and possession of, the humility of the Lamb of God that we are made ready to receive God’s indwelling in full.

Whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Jesus Himself is the proof that these words are true, and He is the guarantee that they will be fulfilled for us. Let us take His yoke on us and learn from Him, for He is gentle and lowly in heart. If we are willing to stoop to Him as He has stooped to us, He will stoop to each of us once more, and we will find ourselves yoked with Him on equal terms.

As we enter more deeply into the fellowship of His humiliation — whether we humble ourselves or bear being humbled by others — we can count on the Spirit of His exaltation, “the Spirit of God and of glory,” resting on us. The presence and the power of the glorified Christ will come to those who are humble in spirit.

When God can once again have His rightful place in us, He will lift us up. Make His glory your concern by humbling yourself, and He will make your glory His concern by perfecting your humility and breathing into you, as your lasting life, the very Spirit of His Son. As the life of God fills you through and through, nothing will feel so natural and nothing so sweet as being nothing — with no thought or wish for self, because everything is taken up with Him who fills everything. “Most gladly will I glory in my weakness that the strength of Christ may rest upon me.”

Friend, isn’t this the reason our consecration and our faith have achieved so little in the pursuit of holiness? The work was done by self and its strength, under the name of faith. God was called in for the sake of self and its happiness. And — unconsciously, but truly — it was in self and its holiness that the soul rejoiced. We never knew that humility — complete, lasting, Christlike humility and self-effacement, running through and marking our whole life with God and with people — was the most essential element of the holy life we were seeking.

It is only in possessing God that I lose myself. Just as the tininess of a speck of dust dancing in a sunbeam is seen against the height, breadth and glory of the sunshine, so humility is taking our place in God’s presence as nothing but a speck of dust living in the sunlight of His love. He says to us: “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” Isaiah 57:15.

Let this be our portion! “O, to be emptier, lowlier, Mean, unnoticed, and unknown, And to God a vessel holier, Filled with Christ, and Christ alone!”

Note D. A Secret of Secrets: Humility, the Soul of True Prayer. Until the spirit of the heart is renewed — until it is emptied of all earthly desires and lives in a constant hunger and thirst for God, which is the true spirit of prayer — until then, all our praying will be more or less like lessons set for schoolchildren, and we will mostly say them only because we dare not skip them. But do not be discouraged. Take the following advice, and then you can go to church without any danger of mere lip service or hypocrisy, even when there is a hymn or a prayer whose language is higher than your heart. Do this: go to church as the tax collector went to the temple. Stand inwardly, in the spirit of your mind, in the posture he showed outwardly when he lowered his eyes and could only say, “God, be merciful to me.” Stand there unchanging, at least in your desire, in this posture or state of heart. It will make holy every request that comes out of your mouth. And whenever something is read, sung or prayed that is more exalted than your heart, if you make it an occasion to sink down still further in the spirit of the tax collector, you will be helped and greatly blessed by those prayers and praises that seem to belong only to a better heart than yours.

This, my friend, is a secret of secrets. It will help you reap where you have not sown, and it will be a constant source of grace in your soul. Everything that stirs inside you, and everything that happens to you outwardly, becomes truly good for you if it finds this humble state of mind in you or awakens it.

Nothing is wasted or useless to the humble soul. It is always in a state of divine growth; everything that falls on it is like the dew of heaven. So shut yourself up in this posture of humility; all good is enclosed in it. It is water from heaven that turns the fire of the fallen soul into the gentleness of the divine life, and produces the oil from which love for God and for people takes its flame.

So always stay enclosed in it. Let it be a garment that always covers you and a belt you always wear. Breathe nothing except in it and from its spirit; see nothing except with its eyes; hear nothing except with its ears. Whether you are in church or out of it, hearing God’s praises or suffering wrongs from people and the world, everything will build you up, and everything will help your growth in the life of God. (William Law, The Spirit of Prayer, Part II, p.

121.)

A Prayer for Humility. I will give you a test here that cannot fail and that will try everything for its truth. It is this: withdraw from the world and from all conversation, for just one month. Do not write, read or debate anything with yourself. Stop all the former workings of your heart and mind. And with all the strength of your heart, stand all through that month, as constantly as you can, in the following prayer to God. Pray it often on your knees; but whether sitting, walking or standing, always be inwardly longing and earnestly praying this one prayer to God: “That of His great goodness He would make known to you, and take from your heart, every kind and form and degree of pride, whether it be from evil spirits or your own corrupt nature; and that He would awaken in you the deepest depth and truth of that humility, which can make you capable of His light and Holy Spirit.” Reject every thought except waiting and praying for this from the bottom of your heart, with the same sincerity and urgency with which people in torment long to pray and be set free. If you can and will give yourself up truly and sincerely to this spirit of prayer, I dare to say that even if you had twice as many evil spirits in you as Mary Magdalene had, they would all be driven out of you, and you would be moved, like her, to weep tears of love at the feet of the holy Jesus. (William Law, The Spirit of Prayer, Part II,

p. 124.)

We know the law of human nature: actions produce habits, habits produce dispositions, dispositions shape the will, and a rightly shaped will is character. It is no different in the work of grace. As actions, persistently repeated, produce habits and dispositions, and these strengthen the will, the One who works in us both to will and to act comes with His mighty power and Spirit. The repentant believer has thrown his proud heart down before God again and again, humbling it; that is rewarded with more grace — the grace of a humble heart, in which the Spirit of Jesus has conquered and brought the new nature to maturity, and in which He, the gentle and lowly One, now lives for ever. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and He will exalt you. And what does this exaltation consist of? The highest glory of the creature is simply to be a vessel that receives, enjoys and displays the glory of God. It can do this only if it is willing to be nothing in itself, so that God may be everything. Water always fills the lowest places first. The lower and emptier a person lies before God, the faster and fuller the divine glory will flow in. The exaltation God promises is not, and cannot be, some outward thing separate from Himself. All He has to give, all He can give, is more of Himself — Himself taking more complete possession of us. This exaltation is not like an earthly prize, chosen arbitrarily and with no necessary link to the behaviour being rewarded. No — by its very nature it is the effect and result of our humbling ourselves. It is nothing other than the gift of a divine humility living within us — such likeness to, and possession of, the humility of the Lamb of God that we are made ready to receive God’s indwelling in full. Whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Jesus Himself is the proof that these words are true, and He is the guarantee that they will be fulfilled for us. Let us take His yoke on us and learn from Him, for He is gentle and lowly in heart. If we are willing to stoop to Him as He has stooped to us, He will stoop to each of us once more, and we will find ourselves yoked with Him on equal terms. As we enter more deeply into the fellowship of His humiliation — whether we humble ourselves or bear being humbled by others — we can count on the Spirit of His exaltation, “the Spirit of God and of glory,” resting on us. The presence and the power of the glorified Christ will come to those who are humble in spirit. When God can once again have His rightful place in us, He will lift us up. Make His glory your concern by humbling yourself, and He will make your glory His concern by perfecting your humility and breathing into you, as your lasting life, the very Spirit of His Son. As the life of God fills you through and through, nothing will feel so natural and nothing so sweet as being nothing — with no thought or wish for self, because everything is taken up with Him who fills everything. “Most gladly will I glory in my weakness that the strength of Christ may rest upon me.” Friend, isn’t this the reason our consecration and our faith have achieved so little in the pursuit of holiness? The work was done by self and its strength, under the name of faith. God was called in for the sake of self and its happiness. And — unconsciously, but truly — it was in self and its holiness that the soul rejoiced. We never knew that humility — complete, lasting, Christlike humility and self-effacement, running through and marking our whole life with God and with people — was the most essential element of the holy life we were seeking. It is only in possessing God that I lose myself. Just as the tininess of a speck of dust dancing in a sunbeam is seen against the height, breadth and glory of the sunshine, so humility is taking our place in God’s presence as nothing but a speck of dust living in the sunlight of His love. He says to us: “I dwell in the high and holy place, and also with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly, and to revive the heart of the contrite.” Isaiah 57:15. Let this be our portion! “O, to be emptier, lowlier, Mean, unnoticed, and unknown, And to God a vessel holier, Filled with Christ, and Christ alone!” Note D. A Secret of Secrets: Humility, the Soul of True Prayer. Until the spirit of the heart is renewed — until it is emptied of all earthly desires and lives in a constant hunger and thirst for God, which is the true spirit of prayer — until then, all our praying will be more or less like lessons set for schoolchildren, and we will mostly say them only because we dare not skip them. But do not be discouraged. Take the following advice, and then you can go to church without any danger of mere lip service or hypocrisy, even when there is a hymn or a prayer whose language is higher than your heart. Do this: go to church as the tax collector went to the temple. Stand inwardly, in the spirit of your mind, in the posture he showed outwardly when he lowered his eyes and could only say, “God, be merciful to me.” Stand there unchanging, at least in your desire, in this posture or state of heart. It will make holy every request that comes out of your mouth. And whenever something is read, sung or prayed that is more exalted than your heart, if you make it an occasion to sink down still further in the spirit of the tax collector, you will be helped and greatly blessed by those prayers and praises that seem to belong only to a better heart than yours. This, my friend, is a secret of secrets. It will help you reap where you have not sown, and it will be a constant source of grace in your soul. Everything that stirs inside you, and everything that happens to you outwardly, becomes truly good for you if it finds this humble state of mind in you or awakens it. Nothing is wasted or useless to the humble soul. It is always in a state of divine growth; everything that falls on it is like the dew of heaven. So shut yourself up in this posture of humility; all good is enclosed in it. It is water from heaven that turns the fire of the fallen soul into the gentleness of the divine life, and produces the oil from which love for God and for people takes its flame. So always stay enclosed in it. Let it be a garment that always covers you and a belt you always wear. Breathe nothing except in it and from its spirit; see nothing except with its eyes; hear nothing except with its ears. Whether you are in church or out of it, hearing God’s praises or suffering wrongs from people and the world, everything will build you up, and everything will help your growth in the life of God. (William Law, The Spirit of Prayer, Part II, p. 121.) A Prayer for Humility. I will give you a test here that cannot fail and that will try everything for its truth. It is this: withdraw from the world and from all conversation, for just one month. Do not write, read or debate anything with yourself. Stop all the former workings of your heart and mind. And with all the strength of your heart, stand all through that month, as constantly as you can, in the following prayer to God. Pray it often on your knees; but whether sitting, walking or standing, always be inwardly longing and earnestly praying this one prayer to God: “That of His great goodness He would make known to you, and take from your heart, every kind and form and degree of pride, whether it be from evil spirits or your own corrupt nature; and that He would awaken in you the deepest depth and truth of that humility, which can make you capable of His light and Holy Spirit.” Reject every thought except waiting and praying for this from the bottom of your heart, with the same sincerity and urgency with which people in torment long to pray and be set free. If you can and will give yourself up truly and sincerely to this spirit of prayer, I dare to say that even if you had twice as many evil spirits in you as Mary Magdalene had, they would all be driven out of you, and you would be moved, like her, to weep tears of love at the feet of the holy Jesus. (William Law, The Spirit of Prayer, Part II, p. 124.)
